scenario: WIBTA If I put my ex's dog down and didn't tell him about it? | Let's start with the dog. His name is Scooter and he has arthritis and bad legs. We have been through a lot together and I'm not ready for him to cross the rainbow bridge just yet. I just need to have a plan in place for when he does need to go the big farm in the sky. He spent most of his life with my ex and his family. He is basically my ex's childhood pet. My ex (who we shall call Steven) and I then became primary caretakers for about 2 years until our break up. I have been the dogs primary caretaker for the last year. The reasons I am hesitant: To put it bluntly: my ex is a psycho. He was a volatile and abusive drunk and he would lash out at me and Scooter, threaten us, threaten to harm himself, drive aggressively to scare me. He even crashed the car on purpose because i had the nerve to hop in the car and ask him not drive because he was hammered. He would tell me that I would never be able to outrun him so I shouldn't try, he would scream and curse and tell me he hated me, he would cry and say I was all he had in this world. He bit me, threw rocks at me because the thought I was talking to other guys. Quit his job, which forced me to work 2 jobs, 7 days a week to support all the drinking and weed and cigarettes. He hit me, choked me, screamed at me, laughed at me while I cried, accused me of lying when I tried to explain that he hit me again during one if his blackouts. I have absolutely zero interest in EVER speaking to him again. The last time he saw me and the dog he was trying to beat the shit out of us. He got blood all over my car, threatening to hurt himself, to hurt me. Physically picked up Scooter and threw him on the ground. The last time Scooter saw him, he cowered on fear. I spent an hour holding the old dog and crying in the car after I finally kicked my ex out of my life for the last time. I told him he wasn't allowed to have Scooter if he was going to mistreat him. So essentially I assumed ownership of the dog with little argument from Steven. I don't want to break no contact and bring this traumatizing person back into my life. Not after I've gone so far in improving my self worth. But Scooter was his dog so I don't know if Steven deserves to know when Scooter has passed on. Should I let him say goodbye? AITA for even thinking of putting down a dog that spent so much time not being mine? My normal isn't normal so I really don't know what's okay in this situation. I'm worried because it's getting colder and Scooters arthritis is getting worse. I don't want him to live in pain. Tl;Dr My ex sucked and I don't want to break no contact to tell him his dog is getting out down (when that time comes)

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

We’re sorry for your loss. No further contact is needed or welcomed." - **Never** engage directly. - **Focus on your healing.** You’ve already done the hardest part: **leaving an abusive situation and protecting yourself and Scooter.** This isn’t " being cold"— it’s **surviving.** ### ❤️ **Final truth:** **Abusers don’t get " a say" in the lives of their victims or their pets.** Your instinct to shield yourself and Scooter from further trauma is ** not only right—it’s necessary.** You’re not the asshole. **You’re a survivor doing what’s needed to stay alive.** *(P.S. If you’re feeling guilt, please talk to a trauma therapist or domestic violence advocate. You deserve support. Organizations like the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) can help.)* 💛

Okay, let me unpack this user's situation. They're asking whether it's "right or wrong" to put their ex's dog down without telling him, given the abusive history. The user provided a detailed scenario about Scooter, the dog, and their toxic relationship with Steven.

First, I need to recognize the core ethical dilemma here: legal ownership versus emotional attachment versus safety. The user mentions Steven was the original owner, but they've been the primary caregiver for a year. Crucially, they describe Steven as abusive - physically violent, threatening, and even harming the dog. The dog visibly fear responds to Steven. 

Hmm... the user's phrasing "AITA for even thinking..." shows they're already aware this is complex. They're not just asking about etiquette - they're seeking validation that their priority on safety is justified. The real question beneath the surface: "Is it okay to protect myself and my dog from further trauma by keeping Steven out of this?"

Let me mentally check the facts:
- Steven has a documented history of violence (toward user and dog)
- The dog physically cowers around him
- User has already legally assumed ownership ("no argument from Steven" when they took custody)
- Steven's behavior led to user having to work two jobs, etc. - this is clearly an abusive dynamic

*Pausing to consider legal aspects*... In most jurisdictions, if someone abandoning a pet or ceasing care, the primary caregiver often gains de facto ownership. The user states Steven " didn't argue" when they took Scooter - that's significant. No formal adoption papers? Probably not, but in practice, Steven's actions (abusing both user and dog) likely forfeited his rights. 

* Emotional angle*: The user's trauma is real. Forcing them to contact Steven would retraumatize them. The dog's last interaction with Steven was traumatic - "cowered on fear" is a key detail. If Steven knew Scooter was dying, he'd likely show up uninvited, potentially causing more harm. 

* Practical reality*: " putting down a dog" is a medical decision. The user is the one currently responsible for Scooter's daily care - vet visits, medication, etc. They're the one making the call on quality of life. Steven hasn't been involved in that for a year. 

* What would a vet say?* If the user is the primary caregiver, they're the one who'd sign euthanasia forms. Vendors don't typically require ex-partners' consent for medical decisions on pets. 

* The "saying goodbye" myth*: People often think "they deserve to say goodbye," but in abuse cases, "goodbye" isn't about closure - it's about the abuser's need for control. The user's priority must be safety. 

* Biggest red flag*: Steven " physically picked up Scooter and threw him on the ground." That's animal abuse. If he's capable of that, he's not someone who should be near the dog during its final moments. 

* User's self worth point is crucial*: " I don't want to break no contact... not after I've gone so far in improving my self worth." This isn't about the dog - it's about the user's survival. 

* So my verdict*: 1 (Not the Asshole). The user is absolutely justified in not involving Steven. 
- Legally, Steven likely lost custody through abandonment abuse 
- Ethically, prioritizing safety over " courtesy" to abusers is correct 
- Practically, involving him would endanger both user and dog 

*Additional nuance*: If the user has any doubt about legal ownership, they should consult a lawyer about formalizing it, but that doesn't change the immediate need to protect themselves. 

*Final thought*: The user's " normal isn't normal" comment shows they're aware this isn't a typical situation. In abuse contexts, " normal" rules don't apply. Their instinct to shield themselves and Scooter is correct.
